note: Vol. I No. 14. The month's last issue, and the one that names the Chicago Academy's trustees and puts the town's building supply on a date: David Carver charters the schooner Post Boy for the first two trips of the season and will land lath, shingles and red cedar posts 'as soon as the ice is clear from the Lake'.

claims.notes: THE ACADEMY GETS A BOARD, A SECOND TERM AND A FURNISHED SCHOOLROOM. It commenced its second term on Monday 15 February 1834 — which agrees with the first quarter the paper saw examined a fortnight earlier (1834-02-11, claim c003 there) — and it is now 'under the public funds for schools', so it is a public institution with two departments and not a private class. FOR A RECONSTRUCTION the usable detail is the FITTINGS: charts, maps, globes and other apparatus 'not common in most public schools of the day', which is a room with furniture in it. WHERE IT STOOD IS STILL NOT SAID, in the third notice about it in four weeks. D. GRAVES SITS ON THE BOARD, and he is the same D. Graves whose house the showman exhibited in the week before (1834-02-18, claim c006 there) and that Botsford and Mason are placed against — a tavern keeper on the school's board, which is what a town of this size looks like. The middle trustee's name is illegible and is left inside its bracket rather than guessed.

claims.notes: THE EARLIEST WITNESS THIS CORPUS HAS FOR BOTSFORD ON THE CORNER OF DEARBORN AND LAKE, five months before the July 1834 card the gazetteer took the address from. The stock is imported — 'direct from Detroit' — and the card announces that the MANUFACTURE of tin will begin at the opening of navigation, which dates a workshop to the spring of 1834 and says it was not one yet. A tinsmith needs a bench, a stove and a shop front; none of that is described and none is supplied. Botsford is placed a second and different way a week earlier — 'next door to Graves'' (1834-02-18, claim c005 there) — and that claim carries no business block so this corner, the better-witnessed address, is the one the gazetteer compiles.

claims.notes: WHERE THE TOWN'S BUILDING MATERIAL CAME FROM, AND WHEN IT COULD ARRIVE. This is the most useful advertisement in the month for a reconstruction. It names the STOCK — lath, shingles, red cedar posts and 'all articles in the lumber line' — it names the SEASON, 'as soon as the ice is clear from the Lake', and it names the SHIP: the schooner Post Boy, chartered for the two first trips of 1834, carrying lumber across from Michigan. Read beside the prices current three weeks earlier (1834-02-04, claim c011 there), which sets shingles at $3.50-4.00 the thousand and poplar lumber at $20-23, it says a Chicago building in the spring of 1834 is framed from stock landed off a lake schooner at a stated price, not from timber cut on the spot. His two agents are on the Michigan shore, which is the direction the lumber comes from. WHERE HIS STORE STOOD IS NOT SAID, so the placement class is `none`; the gazetteer already carries a David Carver from July 1834 and this is the same name and the same trade, five months earlier.

claims.notes: THE SAME SMITHY, THE SAME ADDRESS, AND A THIRD READING OF THE LINE THAT CARRIES IT. T-0310 read this standing card on 1834-01-07 and placed the shop 'on Main-[s]treet, n[early] [o]pposite Grave[s]' Tavern'; the February printings say the same thing in three different states of damage — 'varies rather, on Master, at ly / ile Graves Tavern' (1834-02-11 lines 2592-2593), '[at Gra]ves' Tavern' (1834-02-18 lines 2824-2825) and this one, which is the clearest of the three. The claim is made under the SAME business name so the readings compile into one shop. NOTE THE STANDING TENSION AND DO NOT RESOLVE IT: the gazetteer places D. Graves on South Water Street out of a later notice, and this card puts his tavern on Main street, which is in the West Division. Both are the paper's own words about the same man. A placement pass owes this a decision; a reading pass owes it the record.

claims.notes: IMPORTED ENGLISH FOWLING PIECES ON SALE IN CHICAGO IN THE WINTER OF 1834 — double and single barrelled, 'by the first English makers'. Newberry & Dole are already in the corpus from the first issue as forwarding and commission merchants; this is the same firm selling a luxury import over a counter, which is the kind of stock that says what the town's money was doing. Their card is printed with G. W. Dole's name, and G. W. Dole signs for the Trustees of the Town of Chicago on the bridge proposals three weeks earlier (1834-02-04, claim c005 there); the identification is not asserted here beyond the surname the two notices share. NO ADDRESS IS GIVEN and none is supplied.

claims.notes: A POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT RETURN OF OFFICES ESTABLISHED AND CHANGED, dated 1 January 1834, printed as a two-column table the segmenter has crushed to a column of stubs. IT IS CLAIMED FOR WHAT IT IS AND NOT FOR WHAT IT SAYS: the table exists, it is departmental, it is dated, and NOT ONE Illinois office in it can be read with its county and its postmaster beside it in this transcription. No name is minted from it. It is recorded so that a later pass working from the page images knows there is something here to go back for — the same service the letter-list claims do — rather than leaving the month looking as though the Democrat printed no post-office return at all. The heading and the eleven surviving stubs are quoted exactly as they stand.
